name: Rejuran / salmon DNA facial

card.summary: Polynucleotide (PN) skin-booster injections made from salmon DNA, sold as a skin-quality treatment; evidence for appearance use is still thin and mostly unpublished.
card.aka: Rejuran, salmon DNA facial, PN injections, PDRN skin booster, polynucleotide skin booster
card.note: Clinic-administered injectable; public sources describe few published controlled trials, and the registered trials found are comparisons or not yet recruiting.

quick.overview:
A salmon DNA facial is a cosmetic injection treatment in which fragments of fish-derived DNA (polynucleotides, sometimes called PDRN) are placed into the skin by a clinician. Rejuran is the best-known brand. It is marketed for skin texture, fine lines, under-eye skin and general skin quality rather than for filling volume.
It entered looksmaxxing discussion as one of several injectable 'skin booster' options, grouped with other hardmaxx procedures. Registered trials exist for crow's feet and for periorbital and neck uses, but the sources found describe few published, controlled results.
quick.mechanism: Proponents and aesthetic-medicine sources say the polynucleotides stimulate fibroblast activity and collagen production and support tissue repair, and that the injection also hydrates and conditions the skin. Public encyclopedia summaries describe this as a proposed mechanism from recent studies rather than an established one.
quick.risks: Common reported effects of skin-booster injections in general are temporary redness, swelling and bruising at injection sites; as with any injection, infection and allergic reaction are possible. One general source notes that therapeutic polynucleotides can trigger immune activation. Regulation of PN products varies by country, and no skin-specific safety dataset exists.

lead: A Rejuran or salmon DNA facial is a cosmetic procedure in which a polynucleotide (PN) preparation, derived from salmon DNA, is injected into or just beneath the skin to improve its quality. The best-known product name is Rejuran, and the ingredient is also referred to as polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN). It is promoted for skin texture, fine lines, under-eye skin and overall rejuvenation rather than for adding volume the way a conventional filler does.[1]

Aesthetic-medicine descriptions say the material is thought to stimulate fibroblast activity and collagen production and to promote tissue regeneration, and report improved elasticity and reduced wrinkles after subcutaneous injection; the encyclopedia summaries do not describe the size or design of the underlying studies.[1] Wikipedia notes that fish-derived polynucleotide is used in aesthetic medicine as a dermal filler.[2]

Several clinical trials involving PN-type products have been registered, including non-inferiority and comparison studies for crow's feet lines and not-yet-recruiting studies of periorbital hollowing and horizontal neck lines.[3][4][5][6][7] In looksmaxxing communities the treatment is discussed as a skin-quality or under-eye option among injectables.

paras: Polynucleotides are chains of nucleotide units, the class of molecule that includes DNA and RNA.[2] In the aesthetic products discussed here the material is derived from salmon DNA and is described as polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN) or PN.[1] Preparations are delivered by a clinician as small injections into the skin, sometimes with a cannula for deeper areas, and the product category is often called a skin booster. Topical gels, creams, serums and masks containing PDRN are also sold, some using plant-based alternatives.[1]

Reviews summarised in public encyclopedias attribute the effects of PDRN to stimulation of collagen production, increased fibroblast activity and tissue regeneration, citing recent studies from 2023 to 2025 [1].

Wikipedia's article on polydeoxyribonucleotide describes PDRN as a mixture of single-stranded oligonucleotides of roughly 50 to 1,500 kDa, originally isolated from human placenta for pharmaceutical use in Italy and now mainly purified from salmon or trout sperm. Its main action is described as running through the adenosine A2A receptor after enzymatic breakdown, raising cAMP, engaging PI3K/Akt signalling and VEGF, and feeding the nucleotide salvage pathway that supports cell proliferation [8]. A 2026 expert-opinion article on Rejuran proposes in addition that polynucleotides form a hydrophilic scaffold-like matrix that may support hydration and tissue remodeling [14].

No skin-specific adverse-event dataset has been published. A general encyclopedia entry notes that therapeutic polynucleotides can trigger immune activation, which may reduce efficacy or cause adverse effects.[1] Injection procedures in general carry risks of bruising, swelling, infection and allergic reaction.

According to Wikipedia, PDRN has been studied for wound healing and tissue repair, including diabetic foot ulcers and tendinopathy, and for anti-inflammatory effects, and in cosmetic practice it is used mainly in Asia as a biostimulator after abrasive procedures such as laser treatment or microneedling [8].

A 2026 expert-opinion article from an international panel of dermatologists and aesthetic physicians lists four applications of Rejuran: skin hydration and rejuvenation, structural support through deep-plane injections, barrier repair in rosacea and eczema, and scar remodeling. The panel reported no cases of granuloma or vascular occlusion in the literature to date and also stated that the evidence base remains limited [14].

A 2026 controlled rabbit study of the ear artery compared three polynucleotide products (Rejuran S, Rejuran HB Plus and Conjuran) with saline and cross-linked hyaluronic acid after intra-arterial injection. All polynucleotide-related flow disturbances were transient, with no persistent emboli at 24 hours and no ischaemia or necrosis on day 7, whereas cross-linked hyaluronic acid produced persistent emboli and tissue necrosis [12].
Published human trials of Rejuran and other polynucleotide fillers for appearance are few, and two of the most directly relevant papers carry retraction notices in PubMed.

A 2014 phase III trial in the Journal of Korean Medical Science randomised 72 patients to receive Rejuran on one side of the face and a hyaluronic acid product (Yvoire-Hydro) on the other for crow's feet, with three treatments two weeks apart and 12 weeks of observation, alongside a mouse study; the paper is listed as retracted [9]. A 2025 randomised split-face study in 218 Asian participants compared a polycaprolactone filler (DLMR01) with Rejuran for crow's feet at 12 weeks and reported non-inferiority of the polycaprolactone product with mild adverse events and no serious ones; this paper is also listed as retracted [10]. The registration of the same trial is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov [3].

Other reports are smaller. A 2024 case series described Rejuran for facial scars and burns, including post-traumatic and post-operative scars, and reported reduced scar visibility and improved texture, sometimes in combination with PRP or botulinum toxin [11]. A 2026 retrospective study of six patients with facial lipoatrophy after steroid-containing lipolysis injections reported that all improved, with three near-complete resolutions, after repeated Rejuran sessions [13].

Registered studies include a 2024 comparison of 60 patients between DMSB01 and Rejuran for crow's feet [4], a 2024 trial in 171 patients of HMM1-022 [5], and two not-yet-recruiting studies of deep-plane Rejuran S for periorbital hollowing and of a dual-plane technique for horizontal neck lines, 30 participants each [6][7]. Registry entries do not report results.

Current research interest, as reflected in trial registrations, centres on periocular and neck skin and on comparing newer polynucleotide products with Rejuran.[4][6][7] Topical and plant-based PDRN alternatives are also being marketed.[1]

The treatment was added to the wiki as a hardmaxx option associated with PN injections. It is discussed by people interested in under-eye and skin-quality improvement as an injectable that aims to improve skin rather than reshape structure.

timeline.event: Phase III trial of Rejuran versus a hyaluronic acid filler for crow's feet published (listed as retracted) [9]
A non-inferiority trial of a polynucleotide-type injectable for crow's feet lines in 218 patients starts.[3]
A comparison of DMSB01 with Rejuran for crow's feet lines and a trial of HMM1-022 begin.[4][5]
Studies of Rejuran S for periorbital hollowing and PN for neck lines are registered as planned.[6][7]

angle.text: People use PN skin boosters to improve texture, fine lines and the thin skin around the eyes. It is aimed at skin quality rather than adding volume.
